newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia mine victims ask Diana to bring world ban.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia mine victims ask Diana to bring world ban.

text.p: Landmine victims in Bosnia appealed to Britain's Princess Diana on Friday to help rid the world of mines and said after having dinner with her that they hoped she would take their message to the world.

Diana met 20 Bosnian mine victims and their families over dinner in the northeast town of Tuzla after a private meeting with Franjo Kresic, a former soldier who lost his leg in a mine blast during the country's 1992-95 war.

"What I saw today was her soul," Kresic told reporters after the meal. "Even if you cannot see very clearly you can very distinctively feel what is behind. There are very few people in the world who have what she has."
Kresic lost his sight and both legs after an anti-tank mine exploded on Majevica mountain near Tuzla. He can now see after 14 operations and a double eye transplant from Britain.

"I am impressed by the Princess...I hope that her respect and her influence will result in a contribution that would lead to a decision on a final prohibition and destruction of all types of mines," he said.
Looking tanned and fit in a pale blue shirt, blue blazer, cropped jeans and flat suede pumps, Diana beamed as she came out of the hotel and quickly climbed into her car and drove off.

Her trip came at a time when speculation about her love life hit new heights with London tabloids splashing photos of her with film producer Dodi Fayed, son of Egyptian tycoon Mohammed Al-Fayed, who owns London's luxury department store Harrods.
Her marriage to British royal heir Prince Charles ended in divorce in 1996 after 15 years.

The 36-year-old princess, trying to promote her role as a roving humanitarian ambassador, had planned to highlight the plight of mine casualties in a three-day visit to Bosnia, all of it in the territory of the mainly Moslem-Croat Federation.

"We launched an appeal to the Princess and asked her to give this message to the rest of the world on our behalf," said Plamenko Priganica, another mine victim who chaired the dinner meeting. He said the victims were hoping for more money to help clear the mines from Bosnia.
Newspaper reporters were more interested in uncovering her friendship with Fayed than in learning about the millions of mines still scattered around Bosnia.
"Whatever (the) other distractions are, she puts her mind on what she's doing. She is in excellent form," her friend Lord Deedes told reporters.
Diana met the mayor of Tuzla, Selim Beslagic, who is known for promoting co-existence among Bosnian Moslems, Orthodox Serbs and Roman Catholic Croats.
Diana was invited to Sarajevo by the Washington-based Landmine Survivors' Network, which tries to raise funds for mine victims and to promote a ban on the weapons.
Ken Rutherford, American co-founder of the network who lost both his legs in Somalia in 1993, said after the dinner that Diana would make a "huge difference" to the cause.
He said she knew all about the subject and had taken copious notes throughout the meal. "She's not faking. I'm a landmine victim myself and I know when people are faking."
Diana dined on stuffed vine leaves, shish kebab and an apple and walnut desert at the hotel.

She was making her second trip to a former war zone in her anti-mine campaign. The first, to Angola in January, brought home to many around the world the terrible toll inflicted on civilians by the millions of anti-personnel mines left behind by war.

Diana was not expected to visit Serb-controlled territory in Bosnia, where anti-British feeling is running high after an operation by British special forces to arrest two Serbs wanted by the United Nations war crimes tribunal.
One of the suspects was shot dead while resisting arrest while the other was apprehended and sent to The Hague for trial.
